newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican ruling party members decry government line.
newsitem.headline: Mexican ruling party members decry government line.

text.p: Ruling party activists opposed to the government's free-market policies rebelled at a key party convention on Saturday, demanding a return to the party's socialist roots in the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution.

Through shouts, clenched fists and fiery speeches, delegates of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has governed Mexico without a break since 1929, vented their fury at the foreign-educated technocrats who they say have betrayed party principles in government.

Since 1982, three successive PRI presidents of Mexico have broken with the party's left-wing, nationalistic past to encourage free markets, economic orthodoxy and foreign investment. Many rank-and-file party members have had enough.

"Block the way of the technocrats!" and "We need a revolutionary, nationalist spirit!" were the rallying cries heard repeatedly from the podium, received with roars of "Hard, hard, hard!" from the audience.

One speaker, Rafael Garcia Vasquez, of the state of Baja California, won ecstatic applause for his accusation that by allowing the conservative opposition PAN party win its first-ever governorships over the past decade, the PRI had "done deals with the forces of reaction" and "fallen victim to the fascist right."

The aggressive stance of many delegates on Saturday, the second day of the PRI's 17th National Assembly, marked a dramatic change from previous PRI assemblies, which have generally been stage-managed affairs designed to shore up the government of the day.

Delegates at a session on party statutes approved a proposal to oblige future presidential candidates to be PRI militants of at least 10 years' standing who have won at least one elected job -- a rule that would have excluded President Ernesto Zedillo (himself a foreign-educated technocrat) if it had been in place for the 1994 presidential election.
Analysts said the decision was likely to shatter a half-century-old Mexican tradition under which the president of the day nominates his successor from within his Cabinet.
Zedillo's name was conspicuous by its absence during the first two days of the assembly, though he was scheduled to address its closing plenary session on Sunday.
Delegates were far more concerned with Luis Donaldo Colosio, the PRI's original candidate for the 1994 presidential race, who was assassinated months before the election.

Copies of Colosio's ideology and political proposals were handed out to all delegates, and any speaker who identified himself with the Territorial Movement, a grass-roots party organisation set up by Colosio, was cheered ecstatically.

Many PRI militants believe Colosio's murder was a political plot hatched at some level of the government, but the party leadership tried to keep the delicate topic off the agenda in the interests of party unity.

When Ramiro de la Rosa, from the Democracy 2000 reform wing of the PRI, accused former President Carlos Salinas of being a "thief and a murderer" responsible for Colosio's death, he was grabbed, dragged off and thrown out of the hall.

A later session on party statutes broke down completely as delegates jeered a senator, Eduardo Andrade, when he accused them of creating a "dangerous impression of a break with the president of the republic," Zedillo.
The committee chairing the meeting switched off the podium microphones while Andrade spoke, infuriating the senator, who attempted to snatch another microphone from the chairman.

Chaos ensued as reporters invaded the stage and delegates rose to their feet to boo and whistle at Andrade, who admitted that he had been sent by the party leadership to give his message to the delegates.

PRI president Santiago Onate had to rush in and suspend proceedings to allow tempers to cool before the meeting continued. But in a sign of the hardliners' strength, the group chairing the meeting was replaced with a lineup more acceptable to the rank-and-file militants.

Other party meetings on Saturday were considering whether to expel Salinas, whose 1988-94 administration was the prelude to Mexico's December 1994 economic crash, and oppose the privatisation of the petrochemical industry, a Zedillo policy.
